| [LIT-532](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-532.md) v2 | Inadequacy of entropy and entropy derivatives in characterizing the steady state | Landauer (1975), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevA.12.636. Per its abstract: in a bistable system the kinetics of transitions between the two locally stable states can be changed without changing the behaviour near either state, so no quantity that characterises only the vicinity of the states can determine which is more probable. Separately, even a monostable linear circuit's steady state need not be one of minimum entropy production. Unread: filed from the abstract. | Unavailable — seeded 2026-10-02 from its abstract and Crossref metadata, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (Physical Review A, closed; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex list no open copy). Filed because it is the classic objection to entropy-based characterisations of nonequilibrium steady states, Prigogine's minimum principle among them; it stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-534](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-534.md) v2 | Order Out of Chaos: Man's New Dialogue with Nature | Prigogine & Stengers (1984), Bantam; based on their La nouvelle alliance. A book for general readers that sets the science of complexity and irreversibility against classical dynamics. By its contents: the rise and limits of Newtonian science and its philosophical reception (Diderot, Kant, Hegel, Bergson, Whitehead); thermodynamics from Carnot to Boltzmann's order principle; linear and far-from-equilibrium thermodynamics, bifurcations and order through fluctuations; and the rediscovery of time in physics. Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records and a partial contents note; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scans of the Bantam and Flamingo printings are lending-only, HathiTrust is search-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the popular and philosophical statement of the programme whose technical core is the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)); what it argues, beyond its contents, is not recorded here. |

| [LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md) v4 | Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility | Fischer & Ravizza (1998), Cambridge University Press. Unread seed. The most influential reasons-responsiveness theory of moral responsibility. Responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control (the control that involves alternative possibilities), and Frankfurt-type cases show the two come apart. An agent has guidance control of an action when it issues from her own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism: regularly receptive to reasons, including moral ones, and at least weakly reactive to them. The mechanism is her own when she has taken responsibility for it, which makes responsibility historical. Guidance control so described is compatible with causal determinism, which is the position Fischer calls semicompatibilism. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, from Crossref's book and chapter records, the chapter openings Cambridge Core displays, the record's second-hand readings, the SEP entry Moral Responsibility ([LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md)) and Fischer's own summary in "Stories and the Meaning of Life" ([LIT-689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-689.md), read), not read. No lawful full text was found: the book is paywalled at Cambridge Core, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy (oa_status closed, no repository holding). The shorter work the record's book rule asks for is the authors' own précis (Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 61(2), September 2000, first page 441, DOI 10.2307/2653660), also closed: JSTOR answered with a bot challenge, so I stopped there. A person with Cambridge Core or library access can supply the book (Cambridge UP, 1998, DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511814594); chapters 2, 3 and 8 (pp. 28–91 and 207–239) are the parts to read first, and the short précis is the quickest way to an Active reading. | [LIT-1005](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1005.md) v2 | Social Cognitive Theory: An Agentic Perspective | Bandura (2001). Social cognitive theory's account of people as agents of their own functioning, not only products of their circumstances. The core features of agency are intentionality, forethought, self- reactiveness and self-reflectiveness, and beliefs of self-efficacy are the foundation of it. | [LIT-1006](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1006.md) v3 | Living without Free Will | Pereboom (2001). Defends hard incompatibilism. Moral responsibility in the basic-desert sense is incompatible with determinism and with the indeterminacy of standard quantum mechanics. Agent-causal libertarianism may be coherent and would secure it, but we have no evidence for the indeterminacy it needs, so we have no evidence that we are morally responsible. Frankfurt-style cases defeat alternative-possibilities conditions but not the core incompatibilist condition on an action's causal history. Chapter 4's four-case argument holds that determination threatens responsibility no less than covert manipulation does. The cases themselves are as standardly reported (an agent manipulated by neuroscientists, through programming and upbringing, to ordinary determinism) and were not read here. The record meets the argument secondhand ([LIT-294](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-294.md), [LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md), [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md)). Read in part: the Introduction and Chapter 1 pp. 1–10. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-12 and read only in part: the Introduction (pp. xiii–xxiii) and Chapter 1 pp. 1–10, from the front matter and excerpt that Cambridge University Press publishes for the book (assets.cambridge.org), read in full in [NOTE-823](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-823.md) (Skimmed). What was seen is the abstract, on the SIGIR '98 abstracts page that Moffat hosts at the University of Melbourne (people.eng.unimelb.edu.au/ammoffat/sigir98/abstracts/mitra.html), read through a web-fetch tool that paraphrases, so no quotation from it was checked by script. As paraphrased, the abstract says that adding terms to short queries by ad hoc feedback improves retrieval, that the authors refine the set of documents feedback is drawn from, first with manually formulated Boolean filters with proximity constraints and then with a fully automatic method based on term co-occurrence, and that this "often prevents the query drift caused by blind expansion", improving average precision and precision in the top twenty documents, with the automatic method competitive with the best manual one at little added cost. So the paper uses the term query drift and places its cause in blind (pseudo-relevance) expansion; that the mechanism is non-relevant documents in the top-ranked feedback set, the collections used and the sizes of the gains are not confirmed and need the full text. Nothing seen contradicts the entry's summary or what [TERM-056](../../../record/terms.d/TERM-056.md) and [CLAIM-301](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-301.md) cite it for: query drift with the information need held fixed. |
